children: India’s banking system is sitting on more than Rs 11 lakh crore of surplus liquidity, a build-up that could intensify competition among banks for corporate borrowers and give highly rated companies greater bargaining power on borrowing costs, according to debt-market experts.

Vinay Pai, managing director and head of fixed income at Equirus Capital, expects the immediate impact to show up in refinancing and repricing of corporate debt as banks look for avenues to deploy the additional liquidity.
“I expect the first impact to be a refinancing and repricing cycle, particularly among highly rated corporates, rather than a broad-based compression in corporate lending spreads,” Pai said.

It could allow stronger companies to refinance existing loans, negotiate finer spreads or switch lenders. Some borrowers could also consider replacing expensive foreign-currency debt with rupee loans, Pai said.
India Ratings and Research expects a more limited impact, saying the current liquidity surplus could prove temporary as the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) moves to absorb excess funds.

“We believe the excess system liquidity is a temporary phenomenon and will not last for long, as the recent RBI actions already suggest that excess system liquidity will be withdrawn,” said Karan Gupta, director and head of financial institutions at India Ratings and Research.

The contrasting views point to the central question created by the sharp build-up in banking-system liquidity: how much of the additional money will translate into cheaper and more readily available credit for India Inc?
Borrowers gain
The liquidity build-up follows the mobilisation of $136.38 billion under the RBI’s special foreign-exchange measures by August 31.

Of this, $127.23 billion came through Foreign Currency Non-Resident Bank [ FCNR(B)] deposits. Overseas foreign-currency borrowings by banks accounted for another $5.26 billion, while $3.89 billion was mobilised through the external commercial borrowing (ECB), route, according to RBI data.
The distinction between these routes is important because they have different implications for banks and corporate borrowers.

FCNR(B) deposits are foreign-currency deposits raised by Indian banks from non-resident Indians. The RBI’s special measures encouraged banks to mobilise these deposits and provided hedging support, allowing the foreign currency raised to be swapped into rupees without banks having to bear the full market cost of hedging the currency exposure.

That resulted in a large addition to rupee liquidity. The response was strong enough for the RBI to close the FCNR(B) window on August 31, a month ahead of the original schedule. The facilities for overseas foreign-currency borrowings and ECBs remain open until December 31.

The ECB route is different. These are overseas loans raised by eligible Indian entities, including companies, from recognised foreign lenders or international markets. They are therefore primarily a corporate funding route rather than a source of deposits for banks.

Only $3.89 billion had been mobilised through the special ECB facility by August 31, compared with $127.23 billion through FCNR(B) deposits. This means the overwhelming share of the foreign-currency mobilisation that has transformed banks’ liquidity position has come through FCNR(B).
For banks, however, the resulting liquidity should not be viewed as costless money.

Pai said FCNR(B) deposits were raised at interest rates of around 6-7 percent. The RBI’s hedging support improved the economics of raising foreign-currency deposits by reducing the currency risk and associated hedging cost for banks, but lenders still have to earn an adequate return over the interest they are paying depositors.
That puts a floor under how aggressively banks can reduce corporate lending rates.

image.alt: What the FCNR B fuelled liquidity glut means

children: At the same time, the sheer volume of liquidity gives banks an incentive to find assets on which those funds can earn a return. According to debt-market experts, that is where highly rated corporate borrowers could gain.

Pai said banks could refinance existing high-cost corporate loans, take over loans from competing lenders or acquire assets from non-banking financial companies. Highly rated corporate bonds could also attract demand from banks looking to deploy funds.
For large companies, analysts said, this could translate into greater negotiating power.

A highly rated borrower with relationships across several banks could seek lower rates from existing lenders or invite competing banks to refinance its loans. Companies could also choose between bank loans and corporate bonds depending on where financing is cheaper.

In effect, analysts expect the liquidity surplus to create something resembling a borrowers’ market for the top companies of corporate India even if lending rates do not decline sharply across the banking system.
Pressure on Lending Rates, Credit Demand Strong

There are already signs of greater pressure on lending rates. On September 7, HDFC Bank cut its marginal cost of funds-based lending rates by 5-10 basis points across tenures. A senior bank official said persistent excess liquidity was likely to encourage banks to lend more aggressively and would have an “overhang on interest rates”, the Financial Express reported on September 7.

Credit demand has nevertheless remained strong. Bank credit was growing at 18.3 percent year-on-year as of August 15, suggesting banks have avenues to deploy at least part of the additional liquidity without indiscriminately cutting lending rates.
Pai said credit growth had accelerated from around 12 percent in September 2025 to 14.5 percent in December, 15.9 percent in March and 18.3 percent by June 2026.

Gupta of India Ratings expects the additional liquidity to reduce pressure from elevated loan-to-deposit ratios for a few quarters, but believes the scope for a broad fall in corporate borrowing costs is limited because bank lending spreads are already compressed.
RBI Measures
There is another constraint: the RBI does not appear willing to allow the entire surplus to remain in the banking system.

It has stepped up variable rate reverse repo (VRRR) auctions to absorb excess liquidity. On September 7, it mopped up more than Rs 6 lakh crore through two such operations. Banking-system liquidity was estimated at around Rs 11.16 lakh crore in surplus as of September 6.

The liquidity operations create a countervailing force. Banks have considerably more money available today, but how aggressively they compete for loans will partly depend on how much of that surplus the central bank ultimately absorbs.
Domestic vs Overseas Debt
The glut could also change another part of India Inc’s borrowing equation — the choice between domestic and overseas debt.

For companies without substantial dollar revenues or another natural currency hedge, the true cost of an overseas loan includes not only the interest rate but also the cost of protecting against currency movements.

“The US 10-year Treasury yield is around 4.8%, and markets are reassessing the path of US interest rates following recent economic and employment data. Dollar funding remains relatively expensive; therefore I expect some refinancing of foreign-currency borrowings into rupee debt,” Pai said.

Debt-market experts said companies without natural dollar hedges could therefore consider replacing overseas borrowings with rupee loans if competition among domestic banks makes the all-in cost of local funding more attractive.
Companies with substantial foreign-currency revenues would have less reason to switch because those earnings provide a natural hedge against their overseas liabilities.

The liquidity surge could therefore influence not just the price of corporate debt but its composition — which banks companies borrow from, whether they choose loans or bonds, and whether they borrow domestically or overseas.
Capex question
Whether the liquidity eventually translates into a broader corporate investment cycle is much less certain.

Pai expects the additional liquidity to support corporate borrowing and capital expenditure over the medium term, with housing, manufacturing and infrastructure among the sectors that could benefit from easier availability of long-duration financing.
India Ratings is more cautious.
Gupta said corporate credit growth has improved, although part of the increase reflects higher working-capital requirements resulting from commodity-price inflation.
“While we believe that corporate credit growth is likely to sustain, a liquidity-driven capex cycle is unlikely,” he said.
Analysts said the distinction is important because the availability of credit is only one factor determining corporate investment.

Companies typically undertake large capital expenditure when they have sufficient visibility on demand and believe that additional capacity will generate adequate returns. Easier financing can improve the economics of a project, but abundant liquidity by itself does not create the demand required to justify new capacity.
The RBI’s continuing liquidity absorption also raises questions over how long the present conditions will persist.

On September 7, the central bank’s Rs 7 lakh crore, 30-day VRRR auction attracted bids of only Rs 2.59 lakh crore, while an overnight Rs 5 lakh crore auction subsequently attracted Rs 3.53 lakh crore. The preference for shorter tenures indicates that banks remain reluctant to lock away excess funds for extended periods.
For India Inc, analysts therefore expect the immediate impact of the liquidity glut to be felt more in financing than investment.

Highly rated companies could use competition among banks to refinance existing debt, negotiate finer pricing, change lenders and potentially replace some foreign-currency borrowings with domestic loans. Lower-rated borrowers may see considerably less benefit as banks continue to price for credit risk.

A broader capex cycle will require more than banks having money to lend. It will depend on demand visibility, capacity utilisation, corporate confidence and how much of the current liquidity surplus the RBI ultimately allows to remain in the system.
For now, Pai expects the clearest impact to be a refinancing and repricing opportunity for India’s strongest corporate borrowers as banks compete to put their surplus liquidity to work.

title: Rs 11 lakh crore liquidity glut: What the flood of money in banks means for India Inc
